turn.question_text: Design an offline warehouse layering scheme for one billion events per day; explain each layer and the trade-offs.
turn.expected_answer_text: ODS ingests raw events to keep replay capability. DWD cleans and standardizes schemas, partitioned by event time. DWS does light subject aggregation to control data growth.ADS serves reporting. Trade-off: DWS granularity sacrifices some detail flexibility for query cost; I chose event time over ingestion time so late events land in correct partitions.

turn.question_text: Follow-up: how exactly do you handle late-arriving events?
turn.expected_answer_text: A bounded out-of-orderness window: inside the window we backfill the event-time partition; beyond it, events go to a side table merged by a daily compensation job, and the compensation rule is documented downstream.

turn.question_text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate at Novalake Analytics.
turn.expected_answer_text: My mentor wanted to add a column for backward compatibility directly; I argued for documenting field semantics first. We compromised: wrote the semantics doc, shipped his approach, and I owned regression verification.

turn.question_text: Walk me through the data sync project on your resume.
turn.expected_answer_text: Situation: our team owned daily order sync into the warehouse. Task: I took over dedup and latency. Action: unified field semantics across three upstream tables, rewrote dedup in Python, split the serial job into four parallel shards. Result: P95 latency dropped from ~40 to ~8 minutes, zero failures in two months.

turn.question_text: Your resume shows a gap from March to September 2024. What were you doing?
turn.expected_answer_text: That was my capstone period: I built a real-time dashboard on a public dataset and published three technical blog posts; I started interviewing in late September.
